speechtext:
There were a couple of other speeches, one by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) and one by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), both of whom said that we have nothing really to fear from the Americans; they have no aims on our country and all they want to do is to deal as businessmen. That may be so, and I do not dispute it, but I wish I could be as sure of that as these hon. members are because there are other people around who are not that sure. I should like to quote someone of their own ilk. This article appeared in the Toronto Telegram of October 8. It was written by Aaron R. Einfrank who, the Toronto Telegram alleges,-at that time at any rate it was not a Liberal newspaper-to be an expert on things in Ottawa. He wrote:
The surcharge and other protectionist moves against Canada are indications of the change which has been brought home to me during ten days of interviews in Washington . ..
An example of what might be termed the end of an era is a conversation I had with a high-ranking Nixon Administration Official in his office.
I asked this official, who is close to the ultimate political power in the U.S., what would happen if American protectionist policy led to the destruction of the Canadian state because of resulting economic chaos in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada.
He began his answer in a routine way by saying "I don't think it will happen." Then I was stunned to hear him ramble on: "But if it did happen, it might not be a bad thing."
November 4, 1971

In explaining why "it might not be a bad thing'' for Canada to disappear, he made two points:
The North American economy could be planned on a unified, continental basis, in regard to land and resources, including energy and water, as well as in regard to industrial development.
The addition of 21 million predominatly white "stable" Canadians to the American body politic would counter balance "our minorities here". In other words, these 21 million "stable" Canadians would tend to off-set the influence of 23 million blacks in the U.S.
I do not know whether or not that is correct, but I recommend to the hon. member for Kent-Essex and to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East these comments for their consideration when they are considering the whole problem.
During the course of the debate there has been much philosophizing and much flowing oratory. I should like, if I may in my small contribution, to come down to the facts and face hard realities. What are the facts? I submit that if we really look at them, and look at history, we will admit that Canada and Canadians have been spoilt. We have been spoilt first by the United Kingdom, later by the Commonwealth, and more lately, since the second world war, by the United States of America. We have reached that lofty plateau where we are described as having the second highest standard of living in the world, and I suppose we have. We arrived there, particularly during the last two decades, by looking to the south and seeking to follow as the sheep follow the shepherd. Why do sheep follow shepherds? Sheep follow shepherds because the shepherd takes care of them, and that was what was happening to us during the last 20 or 25 years.
Then came August 15 and the boom was lowered. The shepherd found that his house was in danger. He found that he could no longer take care of all the sheep; he had to look after his own interests, and that is a quite valid position. If he did not look after his own interests, he would be a fool. Some people in this country seem to think that the actions taken by President Nixon on August 15, and latterly by Secretary Connally, are tragedies and represent, in effect, a tragedy for Canada. I do not think so. I think that those activities, and what has happened during the last two months, have given Canada the pause it needed to stop and look at itself. We must must look at our policies, find out where we are, and determine where we want to go. If we re-assess the facts there are two or three things that become obvious.
In order to exist, we must trade. In order to trade, we must have markets. Those markets do not exist in Canada. We need the markets in the United States. We need the markets in the United Kingdom, in Europe, in Russia, in China, in Japan and wherever else we can find them. One alternative, the one that seems to be espoused by the loyal opposition, is that we can seek some form of economic integration, the suggestion being that this economic integration be with the United States of America. One of the members memtioned, and used as an example, the moving by the United Kingdom and other countries into the European Common Market so that that community will now be a group of ten as compared with a group of six. This is the type of example we are told we should follow.
Economic Relations with United States
I should like to point out that it is one thing for six or ten countries of approximately equal size, approximately the same interest in all ways, but particularly in size and particularly in the value of gross national product, to get together and form a bloc. But it is another thing completely for a country the size of Canada to join a country ten times its size and hope to retain any type of national recognition. There is no way that can be done. Economic integration with the United States will lead eventually to complete economic domination, and economic domination will lead to political integration and eventually to political domination as well.

Luxemburg, the three Benelux countries, always work together with Germany as a group and have the same voice as Germany in the Common Market. They are three countries and they work together as one.
A second alternative is to throw up the barriers and take the route to economic nationalism; I think everyone agrees that would be disastrous. A country this size, trying to go it alone, would end up completely on the outside, bankrupt and completely undone, and would be at the mercy of any other country. This, too, would lead to the loss of our national identity.
Thankfully, Mr. Speaker, there is a third route. We, as Canadians, can decide to mature economically. We have been weaned, as I said, by the United Kingdom and by the Commonealth, and to a degree we have received special treatment and pampering from the United States. Now is the time when we should be prepared to recognize that we are no longer economic infants; we are mature people prepared to act responsibly and with maturity.
We must decide if it is possible to enjoy the luxury of having the second highest standard of living in the world and at the same time compete with other countries in the market places of the world. Can we any longer afford the luxuries of wasteful industrial strife, high wages, fat profits large dividends, short work weeks, a high return on the dollar, and so on? Can we afford all that and still claim for ourselves the right to economic and political independence? As responsible adults, what do you do when you realize you are living beyond your means: What then should responsible Canadians do if they wish to retain the right to be called Canadians? That is the question facing us today, Mr. Speaker. Have we matured enough as a nation to recognize and accept our responsibilities? Are we ready to put our work muscles where our mouths are?
We were born a little more than 100 years ago. We took our first faltering steps as a nation when we helped our friends in the Boer War. We passed the age of puberty with flying colours by our participation in World War I. We learned in our adolescence that life is not a bowl of cherries. That was the lesson of the thirties. We demonstrated our strength and daring as young adults in World War II and later in Korea. Now, in a time of crises, in this time of re-assessment, I believe that Canadians have the opportunity to prove to the world and to themselves that they have attained the full maturity of adulthood, and I do not think we should be lacking in the courage to try.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing I want to say is that the speech by the hon.

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) yesterday has drawn consistent and continuous remarks from every member. I cannot understand how a speech which was "so inadequate," "so incomplete," "so contradictory," "so emotional," "so filled with nothing good" could draw such a tremendous response from everybody, beginning with the past leader of the NDP and moving over to the person who sits to the right of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). That struck me as a bit strange when listening to this debate.
In June, 1970, the government published what it termed a theoretical framework of Canadian foreign policy, a white paper which consisted of six booklets: Canada's position on Europe, Canada's position on the Pacific region, Canada's position on Latin America, Canada's position on the United Nations, Canada's position on Development Assistance. But there was no reference at all to Canada's position on her relations with our neighbours, those whom we in this party talk about as our neighbours to the south of us. On numerous occasions we have given the government the opportunity of spelling out its position on economic policies and on other policies connected with our relations with our southern neighbours. We did so again yesterday, and yesterday I listened to the speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). Later, I re-read his speech to see if I could believe my ears and eyes.
His speech contained no reference at all to our present political and economic relations with the United States, no reference at all to the present economic moves by the United States, no reference at all to the Gray Report which finds itself locked away in somebody's desk drawer, no reference at all to energy policies, and no reference at all to the conflicting statements made by people such as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). It was just unbelievable. I have never read or heard so much in my life and learned absolutely nothing from it. The minister's speech was filled with words like "childish". I repeat that this was a speech by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that great diplomat. It was filled with words like "silly," "contradictory," and "hypocrisy," all in reaction to the position taken by our spokesman on external affairs, with no reference at all to the position of the government. There was a continuous challenge, one which seems to be dominant in the front benches of the government, a challenge to our party to state our position on a multitude of issues.
It may be trite to say the obvious thing, Mr. Speaker, that we are living in a unique nation. It is the second largest nation in the world geographically speaking, a nation of 22 million people, a nation with great resources and with great regional disparities but which has a rather unique tariff policy. Our tariff policy reacts to the tariff policies of another government, the government of the country to the south, which has devised a system which makes it difficult for us to manufacture and export manufactured products but which makes it very easy for Canadian industrialists and business people to export raw resources.
Despite the bragging of the government that we have a buoyant economy, we have a country which has had mas-
[Mr. Lundrigan.J
sive problems over the last several years, not just since May, not just since the imposition of the U.S. 10 per cent surcharge, with rapidly growing unemployment. We have a government which has allowed the business community to remain in a position of uncertainty to the point where, if one watched the stock market over the last several months, one saw a drop of 10 to 12 percentage points from the level that existed six or seven weeks ago. According to recent statistics, business failures in the province of Quebec have increased by about 10 per cent and have increased right across the nation.
In November, 1971, we are faced with two significant challenges. The first is to improve our interrelationships with our neighbours to the south through discussions, and the second is to see what we can do within the confines of the Canadian economy, bearing in mind our resources, our manufacturing position, our taxation and tariff position, to help a staggering and sick economy. These challenges have faced this nation for the last several years.
I cannot see how any of those people who sit to my extreme left can say that the motion before us today is the least contradictory. We are saying that we have a challenge to establish healthy working and friendly relationships, both political and economic, with our neighbours to the south. We are also saying that, bearing in mind our resources, the economy of the Canadian nation, the tariffs and the business community, bearing in mind all the conditions that are peculiar to Canada, we can develop economic muscle. That is what we are saying in the motion.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Murphy) was here for 15 minutes today and I heard him and the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) say that we have been spoiled, that we have emerged from puberty and adolescence, have reached adulthood and must become independent. They said we have to become big boys and expose ourselves to all the winds and forces of the international scene, that we have to be able to negotiate with other countries and maybe even turn our backs on our friends to the south, saying that we have now reached the age of maturity. But I ask these members what we have done in the last three years to put muscle in the Canadian economy so that we can become independent, so that we can insult our friends and allow a breakdown in our international relations? Right now we find ourselves in a corner, because at the moment our neighbour receives 80 per cent of our exports.
There are questions that I should like the Secretary of State for External Affairs to answer today. What have we done with energy? Have we found out from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) what our total capacity is? Have we discovered how much the Americans depend on it? Are we in a strong bargaining position? Do we know what our own domestic needs are? Is it necessary to develop the Fundy Tidal Power project? The Churchill Falls project has been developed privately with the assistance of one provincial government and no assistance at all from Ottawa. What is the position on resources domestically? And have the Americans become so dependent on our resources that we can talk tough to them? Have we developed strategies to help our resource
November 4, 1971

industries by means of tax credits, tax abatements, tax incentives or industrial growth incentives? Are the Americans so dependent on our resources that we can take that line of attack without hurting ourselves? Can other nations in the world supply the resource needs of the American people? If we talk tough are we liable to lose the market and thereby the jobs which have been created through the export of raw materials? I feel that this government has reached conclusions on these questions, but for political reasons or through incompetency is afraid to disclose them to the Canadian people.
What is our position on technological capability? Are we so capable technologically that we can forge ahead and become dominant in the world? What have we done about developing managerial capability? The books I have read say that any nation is dependent to a large extent on managerial capability for independence in the industrialized world. Has Canada set up special programs to help business communities, industry, universities and technical colleges develop managerial expertise? I am not talking about a master's degree from a university; I am talking about spending a lot of Canadian dollars to assist the business community in developing competency in the field of management.
What have we done about the recommendations of the Science Council of Canada for a new industrial strategy? I am not referring to an auto pact or an ad hoc policy on textiles or a policy on resources that is ad hoc to everything else in Canada. What I am talking about is a major industrial strategy which includes tax policies, tariff policies, expertise in management. Has the government considered these measures? This is what we are talking about in the second part of our motion when we refer to a number of things that we can do within Canada in order to make ourselves more vigorous and viable. No nation in the world will react to Canada making moves on its own considering its unique characteristics, its qualities, its advantages and disadvantages. This government has not stated any policy on energy, on resource development, on managerial capability nor a new industrial strategy. I do not think that our neighbours to the south can talk with people in this government because I do not believe this government knows where it stands on these issues.

It is an integral part of the Canadian nation in every sense of the word. In the last three and a half years, I think we have had the worst of both worlds. I see members on the other side of the House whose feelings I know are the same as mine. Our economy went from a position of relative strength four years ago to one that is causing grave concern to every Canadian. The economy has been weakened to the point that more than 7 per cent of our labour force, on a seasonally adjusted basis, is unemployed. We have a government that persists in blaming this on our neighbours to the south. They blame everybody. They blame striking workers, single people, young people, the aged, new technologies, lazy deadbeats, organized labour and participation rates; and now they are blaming our United States neighbours for our unemployment.
Instead of blaming all these people, the government ought to accept the challenge of establishing closer and better working relationships with our neighbour to the south and attempt to offset the devastating economic situation that has arisen in Canada. Instead of doing that, we have offended our neighbours. We have made it much more difficult to establish healthy working relationships with them. At home nothing has been done to help us find a way out of our present position in order to make sure that when similar moves are made by other nations in future, the Canadian people will be better able to stand alone. That is the devastating part of what has happened. The challenge facing this government and the Canadian people is this: we must find a better, quicker and easier way to establish adequate working relationships with our neighbour to the south. We must remember that, aside from relying on the United States, we can do many things for ourselves within Canada, so that in future we may stand economically independent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the eloquent and forceful manner in which the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) expressed his point of view, it is entirely clear, of course, that the motion originally introduced by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) is not only confused and illiterate, it is also intellectually dishonest or schizophrenic. That has been clearly established by a number of speakers, including the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland).
I do not intend to spend much time repeating arguments which have been advanced. The motion, however, is helpful and important because it exposes clearly a fundamen-

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
tal cleavage within the ranks of the official opposition. This cleavage cannot be denied and is clear if one reads the record of yesterday's debate. One of the views is that expressed by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) who emphasized the importance of developing, basically, policies of Canadian nationalism. In so speaking, he was speaking in the tradition of the original founder of his party, Sir John A. Macdonald. On the other hand, the hon. member for Hillsborough spoke in another tradition, a tradition which has also been associated with his party for many years, a tradition and I say this with respect because I respect the views of the hon. member, that is based on what I might call the colonial mentality, the fear of independence which pervades a large part of Canadian society and which affects some of our business people, some of our professional people and some of our bankers and other financial people. This is a fear of new initiatives, expressed by the desire to remain in a sheltered position or, as is sometimes said, under the American umbrella. Theirs is the desire to maintain the status quo. After all, these are privileged people and very comfortable at present. They do not want to rock the boat. They are not anxious to take new initiatives. They want to wait and see.
Years ago they wanted to wait to see what Great Britain would do, and then they would follow; and today, Mr. Speaker, they want to wait and see what the Americans will do, and then they want to follow. They are terrified at the possibility that a country so small, so weak and so dependent as they suspect Canada is, should ever do something before our American friends do it. This was made entirely clear in the remarks last night of the hon. member for Hillsborough.
What were the reasons he gave for attacking the present government for alleged anti-Americanism? We had taken an initiative in developing friendlier cultural and trading relationships with the Soviet Union and other countries of eastern Europe. We had taken steps to establish trading and cultural relationships with the People's Republic of China, and we had failed to follow the United States lead with regard to the recognition of the Peking government of China. speechtext:
I suppose all of us in the House have received some of the filthy publications which mostly come, I think, from extreme right wing organizations in the United States which make these charges. I am, in a way, glad to see this charge raised in the House in this

Economic Relations with United States
debate so that the people of Canada can realize just how insubstantial it is.
I should like to return to the most important aspect of this discussion. Should Canada seek economic integration in a single continental American market dominated by the United States, or should we seek economic independence based upon the development of a new Canadian economic policy which in turn must be founded upon the development of multilateral relationships, basically economic relationships? This is the fundamental economic problem which faces us in Canada at the present time. And opinion in Canada is divided right down the middle.
I have spoken of the cleavage within the ranks of the Official Opposition. But there is also a cleavage within the ranks of the NDP. This becomes clear when we emphasize that it is not just business dependence we are talking about but dependence in the field of trade unionism, and the domination exerted by the so-called international unions, which are really United States dominated unions.
Within my own party there are obvious differences of opinion. Although I respect the views of my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Badanai) as expressed earlier today in this debate, I can hardly agree with them.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal attacked the government because it has not yet made up its mind what its policy should be in this field. It has, indeed, taken time to make up its mind and it is just as well that it should not hurry the process. Because when the new policy is published, if it is directed toward achieving a greater degree of Canadian independence, we can be sure that hon. members opposite will attack the government for being anti-American.
Policy in this area has to be developed very carefully and in a responsible way. While continuing to emphasize that we shall necessarily for many years continue to be highly dependent upon our United States friends in many ways, I certainly hope that when the policy is published it will indicate clearly that we are moving toward a greater degree of economic and cultural independence. I hope that we shall reject the notion of complete economic integration with the United States as being inconsistent with the maintenance of an independent and unified Canada.
I should like to emphasize that the new Nixon economic policy involving the 10 per cent surtax and other protectionist devices does pose a serious economic threat to Canada. But it also presents us with a tremendous opportunity if we have the courage to take advantage of it. It emphasizes, as nothing else could, the extent of our dependence on the United States. What is the use of the people of Canada having elections to elect members of this House if our economy is completely integrated with that of the United States: if, as a result, all the basic economic decisions are made in Washington, if at all?
The people of Canada are primarily concerned about their jobs, their families, and getting enough to live decently. All these things are related to the state of the economy. If our economy is integrated with that of the United States, decisions in this area will be made in the United States unless, as sometimes appears to be the case, the U.S. economy is completely beyond the control of the
American people, in which case there would be no one guiding our economy.
For these reasons it is important that the government announce promptly its policy concerning foreign investment in Canada. I hope it will be a policy pointing in the direction of less rather than greater economic dependence upon the United States. Mr. Speaker, to help our United States friends I think we should renounce voluntarily and unilaterally the benefit of the special exemptions they have given us in the past. We should give up our exemptions under the interest equalization tax and other balance of payments programs introduced by the United States to protect its balance of payments position. Our reserves are higher than ever before-more than $5 billion. We could well afford voluntarily to give up the benefit of these exemptions as an indication to the United States that we recognize their problems and wish to help them, while at the same time moving in the direction of greater independence for Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I was beginning to doubt that I would be able to get the floor on this subject today.
I have the pleasure to speak to the non-confidence motion which condemns, and I quote:
the government for failing to employ and improve firm and constructive economic and political relations with the United States, and, at the same time, for failing to develop a new economic policy which would strengthen our economic independence and fully employ our growing and highly-skilled human resources.
I think this motion should be closely scrutinized since it allows us to look back briefly at the performance of the various governments we have had since 1962.
To this end, I will give the substance of the first four speeches I heard in the House. As I only have 15 minutes, I will quote the analysis of those speeches published in today's edition of Le Devoir, entitled "Canada-US hot line cooling down", which states:
The foreign affair critic, Tory MP Heath Macquarrie, yesterday stressed the fact that no Canadian government can afford the luxury of violent anti-Americanism. This statement was booed by the Liberals.
The economies of our two countries, Mr. Macquarrie stated, are closely related, and any government which tries to undermine traditionally good relations between Ottawa and Washington is endangering the position of Canadians, who are in the hands of Americans.
That was for the first speech. The article comments as follows on the second speech:
Secretary of State for External Affairs Mitchell Sharp answered that disagreements between Canada and the United States do not necessarily reflect a deterioration of the relations between the two countries but that they are more likely the outcome of the development of these relations.
These relations must develop according to the circumstances and that sometimes may cause some disagreements, said Mr. Sharp.
He could have added: the extension of their relations with other countries.

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
And I quote further:
For this part, former New Democratic Party leader T. C. Douglas, commended the government for its efforts to establish better relations with the socialist and communist world.
He said that he was surprised to hear that blame from the official opposition which in his opinion goes along with the right wing organizations and newspapers that attempt to accuse the government of turning its back on "our excellent American friends" in favour of the socialist and communist regimes.
However, the NDP member expressed the hope that Canada will achieve greater economic independence and closer control over the corporations operating in its territory.
As we may see, member of the New Democratic Party are always tempted to come back to their socialist doctrine in order to control corporations. So they keep trying to stand against those who dare talk against certain communist doctrines.
As usual, they moved an amendment which was rejected. So, they came up with another one. I want to point out that as far as we are concerned the chair should never accept amendments on allotted days, days which by right belong to the parties moving the non-confidence motion. Often the other parties take that opportunity to try to bring in their own ideas about the motion moved so that it completely loses its meaning, as it happened in our case.
This is why I ask that such amendments not be introduced in future but that we discuss instead the non-confidence motion moved by an opposition party. We should not have to put up with these amendments. Let us deal with the subject matter.
I resume the quotation:
As for Mr. Matte, he stated that we should not wait for a further deterioration of Canada-United States relations before taking action.
Relations are not too good, he went on, compared with what they have been in the past.
Speaking of the Canadian economy, the member for Champlain reiterated that the evil is more in the present system than in the nature of Canada-United States relations.
If Canada could achieve production equal to its consumption, the 10 per cent American surtax on imports would have had little effect on us.
Those were the opinions expressed by the first four speakers on the motion.
Now, let us get down to facts. First political aspects, after which we will deal with our economic situation and finally with our future diplomacy.
To my knowledge, and I have been sitting here since 1962, this matter of anti-Americanism began under the former administration, that of the Progressive Conservative party under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). That government was charged with anti-Americanism because it opened more widely its doors to British goods. That was the opinion of the then right hon. Prime Minister and he may have been right at that. That assuredly did not please the United States because non only did we see the consequences in the progressive conservative defeat, but we all know that the Americans financed the liberal victory. American financiers attempted to bring back to reason those who wanted us to stop relying so much on North American markets.
That is the nature of the present conflict and I do not contend that the Progressive Conservative government
(Mr. Gauthier.]
was any more anti-American than the Liberal government that followed was pro-American, but I say that we acknowledge facts. American capital put the government headed by the right hon. Mr. Pearson into power, because the previous Progressive Conservative government disappointed Americans a little.
The present government under the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) then presided over the destinies of the country. Several questions come to our minds. We feel the United States are also asking themselves questions, because they do not know whether the present government is pro-American, anti-American, socialist, capitalist or democratic. We still do not know. It is neither flesh nor good red herring. I think that is partly what the United States fear. Even those who are members of the cabinet fear that. Privately, they are afriad of the Prime Minister: is he a socialist disguised as a liberal, or a liberal disguised as a financial dictator? We still do not know.
That is, I believe, part of the cause of our present difficulties with regard to our relations with the United States. At times, he says that he is of the left or of the far left, although he looks to the far right and remains with the Liberals. And this governmental instability surely scares the United States, although, on the whole, some effort is made today to find markets outside the American continent-which is very well-but the economic context should not be ignored.
And this brings me to my second point, the economic context in which we find ourselves. What are our present economic positions? In fact, in many areas, especially with regard to raw materials, we are exporters. We also export a certain quantity of semi-finished products, but we import large quantities of finished products, and this poses a threat to our economic situation.
In order to direct our economy toward increased independence, as proposed in the second part of the motion, I feel that it is time for Canada to deal with its own affairs as regards finished products. This is where our economic weakness is most apparent. As long as we are not aware of this economic weakness, we will not be able to live beside a country like the United States and deal with them on equal terms, because we are dependent on them. In fact, we are a little bit like the child who has not yet left his mother; we are still being led by the hand by the United States since we have to get from them 60 per cent of our consumer goods.
If this government really means business, if it wants to act responsibly, let it start first by developing our secondary industries so as to satisfy the needs of local consumers. That is the first step to take.
On the other hand, we often compete with the United States. We should not conceal the fact. As competitors, we should play the game and be cautious. If we are selling the same product to other countries, it gives rise to conflicts because the United States are used to treating us as a child and when we want to act like an adult, they get angry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been said by other hon. members, this Conservative resolution is an embodiment of contradictions. They are trying to have it both ways; they are trying to ride two horses at once. On the one hand they condemn the government for poor relations with the United States because it took certain initiatives, and on the other they condemn the government for not presenting a policy of economic independence, which in itself is a very serious issue that could disrupt relations with the United States. I do not view this as an argument against such a policy and I will discuss this question later. The Conservative opposition condemns the government when it takes steps to make this country more independent, but at the same time criticizes it for not doing more. Fortunately, most Canadians can see through this nonsense.
What are the matters raised by the Conservatives when they allege there are poor relations between Canada and the United States? First of all they refer to the recent economic measures introduced by Mr. Nixon, the surcharge and others. If those measures resulted from Canadian action, certainly all governments in the world could be condemned by the same resolution. I submit, as many others have done before me, that the United States action is an attempt by that government to solve their economic problems by riding on the backs of not only their enemies but also their friends. In that particular instance I say Canada is not at fault. We have floated our dollar, we have had very liberal trade with the United States, and we have tried to communicate on all problems. What has happened is not the fault of this government.
Another issue raised is the Amchitka incident. If there are poor relations between Canada and the United States as a result of our protests regarding the Amchitka test, whom are we to hold responsible? Are we to hold responsible those people who may be damaged seriously by such a blast, or are we to hold responsible those people who are initiating this atomic test which could cause serious ecological and personal damage not only to Canada but to many parts of the United States and other areas of the world? I fail to see how the Canadian government bears any responsibility if there is a breakdown between Canada and the United States on that point.
Next we have the visits of Messrs. Kosygin and Tito to Canada and the visit of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) to eastern Europe. We also have developed relations with China. Again, I fail to see how our initiative in attempting to build bridges between the west and the east for the good of peace in the world can be considered a measure which is anti-American. I fail to see how an attempt by this government to take strong initiatives for the independence of Canada by spreading our contacts and creating friends in many parts of the world can be considered anti-American.
The Conservative position in this regard is just not credible. As has been pointed out, the United States itself has followed up the initiatives we have taken. After we established relations with China, the President of the United States announced that he would be visiting that country. We do not think he will try to establish relations with China, but his visit could lead to that in the long run.
Economic Relations with United States
The President is going to the Soviet Union. Our Prime Minister took the initiative and went there last year; he was the first western head of government to do so.
If in raising these issues the opposition is trying to present them as a policy of anti-Americanism, I fail to see how that can be done. These policies have been followed by the government in an attempt to make Canada more independent economically, politically and socially. As a result of these new contacts in the eastern bloc and in Asia we hope to develop cultural and economic relationships which will be of benefit not only to Canada but to the western world.
There have been other measures taken in the last few years. We have attempted through the Canadian Radio Television Commission to develop a more independent broadcasting policy and we have attempted to develop more independent policies in other areas. For a long time we have maintained relations with Cuba and we have traded with that country although the United States did not do so. No one considers that as being anti-American.
I reiterate that it is in the interests of Canada, since we lie between the Soviet Union and the United States, to establish good relations with both these countries. In this era of modern communication and fast means of transportation the Soviet Union is as close to us, in many respects, as the United States and I think it is necessary that we maintain these close relationships.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the supper hour I had pointed out that the government has taken many new initiatives in respect of foreign policy. We admit that and are proud of it. But as I mentioned before, these have been pro-Canadian policies rather than anti-American. If the United States blames us for helping ourselves and for trying to protect our own interests, then it is doing this as a pretext for carrying on its isolationist policies. We want friendly relations with the United States. It is in the interests of both countries to have friendly relations-but we would not want such relations at the expense of our own interests, our own sovereignty, our own resources, and so on. We feel we can be a close friend of the United States

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
and still be very pro-Canadian. I believe the United States is big enough and mature enough to appreciate and accept such a relationship.
The second part of the resolution condemns the government for failing to develop a new economic policy which would strengthen our economic independence. That is not true: the government is developing such a policy and has taken certain steps already. It has set up the Canada Development Corporation. It has taken action in the case of Denison Mines and Home Oil. Also, several fiscal measures have been adopted. It was a Liberal government which appointed the Watkins commission, and another Liberal government which referred the report of that commission to a cabinet committee. In addition, the Government reported recently through the Prime Minister that it will make its policy on the Gray report known very shortly.
I was a member of the external affairs committee which prepared the report on United States-Canada relations in 1970. I fully support the recommendations in that report and hope that several of them will be included in the government's policy statement when announced. I think it would be worth while to repeat some of the important statements in the report of the external affairs committee. In summing up their assessment of the U.S.-Canadian relations the committee said:
The danger facing Canada is not one of political absorption by the United States: The danger which Canada must guard against is that it will drift into such a position of dependency in relation to the United States that it will be unable, in practice, to adopt policies displeasing to the United States because of the fear of American reaction which would involve consequences unacceptable to Canadians. The committee believes it is in the interests of both Canada and the United States that Canada should remain politically united and economically strong.
The committee has concluded that, in addition to maintaining political independence, Canada must also maintain a sufficient degree of military, economic and cultural independence that it will, in practice, be able to make the independent decisions which constitute the vital characteristic of an independent nation.
This was a report by a committee with a majority of Liberal members. It is true we had support for these recommendations from members of other parties. One important recommendation in the report is that we must adopt positive measures to make our industry much more efficient so that it can compete on a world-wide basis. We also recommended the establishment of a Canadian Development Corporation. That has been set up.
Another important recommendation was that we enact a Canadian ownership law which would set up a Canadian ownership and control bureau. It was suggested that this Canadian ownership and control bureau would monitor foreign ownership, would keep a close watch on foreign companies operating in Canada and would see that these companies follow the guidelines and laws laid down for foreign corporations. It would do many other things which I cannot go into this evening because I do not have sufficient time. One thing it would do would be to monitor a rule which we think should be implemented, to the effect that in key sectors of Canadian industry 51 per cent of voting shares should be in Canadian hands. Unfortunately, this recommendation was misunderstood when the report came out and was badly reported in the press. It was reported that we had recommended that companies operating in Canada must have 51 per cent Canadian

control. That was not the recommendation. The recommendation was as follows:
Nevertheless, the committee recognizes that as a general rule it is desirable that Canadians should control Canadian companies by owning at least 51 per cent of their voting shares particularly in the important sectors of the economy where American control is now most highly concentrated, and that we should move toward this goal as rapidly as capital requirements and other relevant circumstances permit.
The recommendation was that in important sectors of the economy we must maintain control as we acquire the capital. Another important recommendation was that there should be no take-over of a Canadian company unless such take-over is passed by the Canadian ownership and control bureau. This is a very important recommendation. There were others with respect to the extraterritorial effect of American and other foreign laws in Canada, the role of foreign-based trade unions, cultural imperialism, and so on.
I submit that this was an important report. Much time was spent on it. I presume that the government is taking these recommendations into consideration in preparing their economic independence policy statement, in addition to their consideration of the Gray recommendations. I feel that the government has been moving in this direction and I have confidence that soon we will have a strong policy on Canadian economic independence.
In conclusion, I want to state again that I think the motion by the Conservative opposition is a nonsense motion. It is trying to sit on both sides of the fence at the same time. It criticizes the government for the very thing that it asks for in the latter part of the resolution.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot say that there has been a high-level debate from some quarters today, but it has been a very interesting one and it is the first occasion for some time that government members have been really smoked out. Shakespeare had a word for nearly everything and what he said certainly applies to government members-methinks she doth protest too much! I have never seen such an exhibition and heard such pronouncements of how much we love the United States. What a reversal this is from the actions, which speak much louder than words, of the last two or three years. I will deal with those in a moment.
Also very interesting to me was the speech of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland). I am sorry he is not in the House at the moment because I dislike criticizing a member in his absence. I am extremely sorry that the hon. member for Selkirk dealt with the speech of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) in the way that he did. He got himself all wrapped up in pious observations about intellectual honesty. If I recall his speech this afternoon, he described the expulsion of Taiwan from the United Nations-mentioned by the hon. member for Hillsborough in his speech-as a cruel act. He intimated that the hon. member for Hillsborough had said that the seating of the People's Republic of China was a cruel act. Of course, this is pure nonsense.
I am not imputing motives to the hon. member for Selkirk: one cannot do that. I can only assume from what he said and from the evidence that he is new in this House
November 4, 1971

and, I presume, very new to the United Nations and that therefore he probably made a mistake. What the hon. member for Hillsborough said is clearly on the record. I think in the view of nearly all members of the House, if not all, the People's Republic of China should indeed have the Chinese seat in the General Assembly and on the Security Council.
What was objected to by members of this party was that Taiwan, which is a different government altogether and for which the American resolution would have provided a seat, should not have been allowed some representation at the United Nations. They had been a good member of long standing. They had paid their dues better than some other nations. That was promised in the last election by the man who sits in the seat of foreign affairs minister of this country. "Oh, no, we would never sacrifice Taiwan", he said in the nice manner of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). He changed his mind pretty quickly.
I am sorry that the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) is not here, but I was very interested in his mindreading speech this afternoon. All I can say is that it is just another indication of how disturbed hon. members over there are about this whole debate, because everybody recognizes them for what they really are no matter what they say. The hon. member for St. Paul's wanted to know why people in Canada and on this side of the House think the government is anti-American.
I have some examples which I am happy to be able to provide for him. Let us take the following, for example. During the Prime Minister's recent visit to the Soviet Union, in what was I suppose a happy frame of mind after a Russian dinner-you can get in that frame of mind after those dinners-he said that Canada needed to have closer relations with Russia to counterbalance the military threat from the United States. Then, of course, there is the little item of the cutting of our NATO commitments and certain other matters which were dealt with by my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Economic Relations with United States
Forrestall), regarding our lack of co-operation in other defence fields.
Then there was the red carpet treatment given by us to U.S. draft-dodgers. Let us only compare the immigration difficulties presented to good, honest immigrants who wanted to come here from Italy, the Netherlands or elsewhere. They were examined for security and everything else, but the draft-dodgers were cleared, so we were told, sometimes in half an hour. There is also the recent attitude at the United Nations regarding Taiwan. I have already mentioned that. There was the reported behaviour of members of the Canadian delegation jumping with joy, laughing and screaming epithets at the American delegation when the United States suffered the diplomatic defeat which they did. This is bad manners.

This is not a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I am certainly prepared to accept the word of the hon. member for whom I have great personal regard. I realize he was there at the time in his capacity as parliamentary secretary. The only thing I have to say is that I had reports from some of my colleagues who were there, and when the question was raised in the House the other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs seemed a little unsure of his facts on the matter. While there is no question in my mind that the hon. member who has just spoken would certainly not have engaged in such activities, I am informed that some of our other delegates did. Perhaps the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) did not see it.
There are other matters. The division concerning Canadian-American relations is not confined to the government; unfortunately, it also exists among the people of these two countries, with the daily barrage of anti-American propaganda whipped up by some members of the government party and by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in its daily, venomous attacks on the United States.
People in the United States hear this; the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation covers a large section of the United States. Since it is the CBC they think it is the public mouthpiece of the Canadian government. Mr. Speaker, you know that is not so and I know it is not so. We know that the CBC is an entity very much unto itself. But people in other countries do not understand these niceties, particularly when they hear "hate America" propaganda every day.
I remember that at one of the last meetings of the broadcasting committee I asked the president of the CBC if he could produce one program from the public affairs division that had been even neutral to the Americans within the last five years. He had to think for a while and

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
then he said there were two, a series on the American landings on the moon, and de Tocqueville's visit to the United States, which I think took place about 1828.
Then there is confusion about U.S. investment in Canada. We hear "Yankee go home" from all quarters. We heard something like that from a former Minister of Finance, Walter Gordon, a prominent member of the Liberal party, and from others. Yet we do not seem to have any policy. This is something that has been mentioned by a number of members on the other side of the chamber. It must be very difficult for our American friends when we have the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) going down to the United States begging Americans to invest their money in Canada, and then we have the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene)-I am sorry he also is not here-speaking and giving Americans hell for investing here. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is saying much the same thing. This must be puzzling to Americans.
Then we have the provincial premiers, the premier or former premier-whichever he is-of Newfoundland, the premier of Nova Scotia, the premier of New Brunswick and the premier of Quebec going down to the United States asking our American friends to invest in Canada, and when they do and they come up here they get a chorus of "Yankee go home". You cannot blame our American friends for being a little puzzled about where we are going.
I have heard the question asked, "What are you people going to do about it?" The first thing that I suggest the government should do about it is try to produce the Gray report, on which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) spent one dickens of a long time and much hard work, instead of burying it in the recesses of cabinet lockers. Let us have a look at it. The government should formulate a policy on American and other foreign investment in Canada. But the government has done nothing, has shown no indication of doing anything and has not given any leadership other than schizophrenic pronouncements by various cabinet ministers.
We would like a co-ordinated effort in this regard. The government should take the lead in determining our policy on American and other foreign investment. It should hold a conference with the provinces on this matter and, in all fairness to our friends, whether they be in the United States, the U.K., West Germany, Japan or wherever else, the government should say, "This is our policy. We would like your money here under certain terms and conditions. These are the terms and conditions." But we have had none of that, not one bit of it. There has been no leadership. All we get is anti-American propaganda when someone on the other side of the border does something that does not suit the views of this government.
In 15 minutes, Mr. Speaker, it is pretty hard to deal at length with a very complex subject such as Canadian-U.S. relations. But there is very little doubt about one thing. The government says that things are fine and relations have never been better with the United States. But everybody in the country knows that is not so. All we ask the government is this: please try and avoid in the future incidents such as I have mentioned tonight. A recent

example of such an incident concerns the Amchitka explosion. I am sure that nobody in this House approves of nuclear explosions. I certainly do not, and I spent a good many years of my life working at the United Nations on this problem. But some of us object to the selective vilification of the United States. On this point I agree with the hon. member for St. Paul's who spoke this afternoon.
The government of France has announced that it is going to detonate nuclear explosions in the atmosphere next spring. I hope there is the same amount of protest to the French government and in front of the French embassy next spring as there has been in front of the American embassy, and also in front of the Russian embassy, because I point out that the Russians detonated a big nuclear blast last month; and I hope the same thing happens with respect to the Chinese. You can readily understand why people in the United States think the Canadian government is anti-American when it selects the American government for selective vilification and all other governments are allowed to do whatever they like and no one here utters a peep.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there is an old expression which says that it is not what you do, it is the way you do it. No one in any party in this House does not want the Canadian government to stick up for Canadian national interests, but you do not have to be anti-American to be pro-Canadian. It is as simple as that. And it is not in our national interest to be attacking the United States constantly, gnawing at our closest neighbours. They are our closest neighbours whether we like it or not. If a major war breaks out and nuclear bombs are dropped on Detroit, that will affect the whole southern end of Ontario. If dropped on the Seaway, that means Montreal; and if dropped on Seattle, that means Vancouver.
Whether we like it or not, we are tied up intimately with the United States-militarily, economically and in many other ways. The best thing for us to do is to get along with our friends, and they have been our friends at least since 1812. We can be firm with them and we can be severe, but we do not need to be unnecessarily abusive and provocative.

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned, the question of relations with the United States is most difficult. In this country, through two world wars we suffered enormous losses in wealth and materiel but particularly in terms of personnel, people killed. We suffered enormously before the Americans came in. We welcomed American citizens in our armed forces, those who came to fight for what we thought was democracy, for what we thought the two countries, Canada and the United States, stood for even before their government realized this. At this time I think we should bear in mind that there are many Americans then and now who have shown themselves to be friends and who shared our ideals even though their own governments were a little behind.
We realize that in the two world wars it was necessary for many European nations with whom we also have very close links, the United Kingdom in particular, to virtually give away, to sell at fire-sale prices, all their assets overseas to American corporations and American interests. I wonder whether the U.S. today remembers this.
I think it is only fair to point out that we have long experience of a fruitful relationship, but one that was never easy. It was not easy back in 1812 when, as the hon.
Economic Relations with United States
member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) mentioned, we had our difficulties. It was not easy during the Fenian raids or at any other time since then.
I must say I find the present debate very disappointing. We have heard that the Tory party which has abandoned its traditional positions which, incidentally, it held 93 years ago when my great grandfather, the nominated Tory candidate, stood down to allow Sir John A. Macdonald to be elected in Victoria. He did this because he believed in the principles that Sir John A. stood for then. What the Tories stand for now we do now know, and we have not learned a great deal in the last day and a half. All we know is that it is far from their historical position, far from the position of the great Sir John A.

Perhaps more than most, we on this side of the House often see irreconcilable differences among members of the Tory party which, of course, because they are in opposition and intend to remain in opposition, they make no attempt to reconcile or deal with.
The problem facing this nation of how to arrange relations with the United States which takes such an enormous amount of our trade, which has so many Canadian born citizens, which wields more power than any other nation on earth, is an extremely difficult one. To suggest that we can somehow deal with this problem with simplistic formulae, in a trite and trivial manner, is foolish and does no service to good relations between our two countries, which I hope all members of this House are anxious to see in as good condition as possible.
With respect to trade, we understand the American position and their vast balance of payment deficits. They have a war in Indo-China. Perhaps more than most members I realize what a traumatic experience this is for the Americans because I spent a year in Viet Nam in 1963-64. We realize that this war has led to economic difficulties because the United States government was unwilling to finance it by taxing the people. They attempted to finance it by a peculiar form of deficit financing which, to a large extent, I believe, has led them to their present difficulties.
We warned them that the problems they now face might occur. At the same time, despite the criticism of members

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
of the Conservative party and the New Democratic Party, we have attempted to do something about these problems, something to help the United States. For example, over a year ago we freed our dollar and allowed it to float. There were cries of anguish from the opposition that we were hurting the Canadian exporter, yet it was known at that time that this step was necessary in order to prevent the trade situation becoming so unbalanced that the Americans would be forced to do something drastic about it. We tried to act in a reasonable way. We pointed out to them the amount of American ownership in this country. I could refer to the U.S. trade and ownership figures. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
When recently questioned in the House of Commons on the position of Canada-U.S. energy talks, the Prime Minister had this to say:
We are not at this time prepared to continue them because we do not have the wherewithal, the personnel and the time to arrive at a decision.
Obviously, this cannot be true since talks between Canada and the United States have been going on for the last two years and by now Canada should have at least a
temporary position on domestic energy in the continental American market. Furthermore, the reluctance to initiate further talks on energy at this time suggests strongly a veiled threat by the Prime Minister to use Canada's energy exports as a lever to counteract domestic effects of the recently imposed 10 per cent surcharge. Such a posture by the Prime Minister of Canada adds further support to the growing concern felt by many over the deterioration of Canadian-American relations. My following statements proposed to elaborate on this assumption by placing the Canadian position in its proper perspective.
Let me ask, Mr. Speaker, where does Canada stand? Let me give a little background to my remarks. The largest consumer of oil and gas in the world is the United States of America. If I may illustrate, last year the Americans used approximately 15.6 million barrels of oil daily. This year that consumption has risen to 16.5 million barrels daily. By contrast, Canada's daily consumption of oil was about 1.4 million barrels daily in 1969 and last year it was about 1.5 million barrels daily. This year's domestic consumption is about 1.6 million barrels per day.
The largest oil reserves in the world are found in the Middle East, Russia, South America and the United States. May I illustrate. Of total, known world recoverable oil reserves, the Middle East has about 50 per cent, Russia and South America 30 per cent and the United States 10 per cent. By contrast, Canada holds only 2 per cent of recoverable world oil reserves. Furthermore, on the basis of present patterns of consumption, the Middle East has enough oil for the next 50 years, Canada for the next 20 years and the United States for the next 10 years.
As these figures show, the United States has been relying and will continue to rely increasingly on foreign imports of oil and gas to protect her meagre reserves while at the same time meeting rising domestic demands for these commodities. Presently foreign imports of oil and gas to the United States come from essentially three regions, Venezuela, the Middle East and Canada. Of these foreign imports, Canada supplies about 25 per cent of the daily requirements of the United States. In 1969 Canada's exports to the United States stood at about 555,000 barrels per day. By 1970 this export had increased to about 670,000 barrels per day.
On August 15, President Nixon announced the by now famous 10 per cent import surcharge. This surcharge affects about one quarter of Canada's exports to United States markets. The surcharge, however, does not affect the sale of Canadian oil and gas to the American market. In fact, as the latest preliminary figures from Statistics Canada indicate, the export of petroleum in September increased 18.5 per cent and natural gas exports increased about 27.5 per cent. These very large export increases came about one month after the surcharge was imposed and probably reflect the increasing demand and dependence of the American market on Canada's energy fuels.
On October 4, 1971, the Prime Minister indicated to the House of Commons that talks between Canada and the United States on energy, which were adjourned in the spring of this year, have not been resumed this fall because-
-at this particular point we are preoccupied with other matters, particularly economic matters, and .. . we are not in a position at the moment to sit down with United States officials and continue

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
these talks. But there has been no indefinite postponement of them, there is merely an inability to find the time now to proceed with them.
