subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Canadian producers responded so vigorously during the remainder of 1971 that in September, one month after the imposition of the 10 per cent surcharge, Canadian exports of oil and gas to the United States were up 18.5 per cent and 27.5 per cent respectively. Yet despite the prospect of continued sales of more oil and gas to the United States as well as the planning for more formal, long-range agreements between Canada and the U.S. on energy matters, the Prime Minister announced that we were not prepared to continue talks because we did not have "the wherewithal, the personnel and the time to arrive at a decision".
Obviously this cannot be true, since talks between Canada and the United States have been going on for the last two years. By now Canada should have taken at least a temporary position on energy in the continental American market. Furthermore, the reluctance on the part of the Prime Minister to initiate further talks on energy with the United States at this time suggests strongly a threat by the right hon. gentleman to use Canada's energy exports as a lever to counteract the domestic effect of the 10 per cent surcharge.
Canada cannot afford to stop exporting oil and gas to the United States. However, at the same time care must be taken not to overextend domestic reserves and not to ship too much energy to the American market. What is needed now is a comprehensive Canadian energy policy, rather than the threats of our Prime Minister, if we are to stabil-

ize our domestic industry and support better Canadian-American relationships in this vital sector. Let me say that the following points in a Canadian energy policy coijild help to achieve these objectives:
1.	A Canadian energy resource policy should encourage a de-emphasis on any one particular energy commodity by stressing new alternative sources of energy. A better energy mix can be achieved if less reliance is placed on such commodities as oil and coal and if such new sources as tides, chemicals and wind are tapped.
2.	Energy should not be treated solely as a commodity available for export but as a factor of production in the Canadian economy. Because of its unique role in our economy, better energy balances must be achieved between regional production and consumption and between domestic and foreign consumption.
3.	Present thermal systems can convert fossil fuels to electricity at 40 per cent efficiency. New technologies can do the same at 55 to 60 per cent efficiency. Canada must develop these new technologies to conserve her domestic fuel supply.
4.	Of the five conventional energy sources, hydro, uranium, coal, oil and gas, coal is the most abundant in Canada. Because of escalating energy demands Canada must convert more extensively to the use of coal.
5.	A Canadian energy resource policy must attempt to achieve better regional and northern development. To this end attempts should be made:
a)	to forbid any mineral extraction from areas north of the treeline while at the same time encouraging more exploration in these regions;
b)	to develop a government assisted program for mid-Canada which will build up suitable industries in northern communities once the mineral extractive phase is over; and
c)	to achieve a more balanced approach to oil and gas exploration in Canada's marine and offshore areas.
6.	No attempt should be made to enter into any longterm continental energy arrangements with the United States. At the same time, no attempt should be made to exert leverage on the United States by not exporting any more oil and gas to these markets.
We in the House of Commons have had our eyes opened. We have been told by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that Canada-U.S. relations are on a firm and reliable basis because our grey-flannel diplomats are more on the ball than ever before. All must be well because our diplomats and our officials are talking as they have never talked before! Mr. Speaker, I am still not impressed, because I do not believe diplomats and cocktail parties have, will or can formulate constructive and self-interested foreign policy to protect and maximize Canadian-made interests within North America.
The talks and contacts the present government has had with U.S. officials over the last three years have, by and large, been ad hoc, superficial, inconsistent and indecisive. Our diplomacy with the United States is simply an extension of this government's performance at home. Now, because diplomacy cannot function in a vacuum, the real crux of the issue is the fundamental and original failure of the Trudeau government to develop a new eco-
November 4, 1971

nomic policy for the most beneficial and independent development of the Canadian economy.
While the machinery and competence of Canada's diplomatic efforts in Washington must and can be improved, it is na'ive and dangerous to suggest we can construct optimum Canada-U.S. relations before we decide what are the best goals for Canada. Diplomacy is at best a servant of Canadian goals. Therefore, we cannot have an effective and coherent diplomatic strategy without an effective and coherent strategy for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is here that the Trudeau government has neglected my country's interests and squandered our opportunities.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The present government is not equipped to negotiate a practical and reliable energy policy with the United States because it has failed to formulate a comprehensive energy policy for Canada. The government is not equipped to negotiate an end to the surcharge or a constructive new trade policy with the United States because it has not succeeded in formulating an industrial policy, an employment policy or a regional and national development policy for Canada.
The government has been unable to take leadership in the IMF or in the Group of Ten talks on trade and currency reform because it has formulated neither an optimum dollar nor an optimum trade strategy for Canada. Simply, it cannot reach out to the United States or to the world. It cannot bargain and it dare not bargain, because it has no policy for Canada.
If the government is to stop compromising our longterm interests and moving from crisis to crisis and inconsistency to inconsistency in its relations with the United States, it must first stop doing the same with Canada. It is of first priority that the government come clean with Parliament and the provinces of Canada and develop a new economic policy. The government must construct an industrial policy, a trade policy, a foreign investment and capital policy and an energy and human resource policy. With such new economic policy for Canada it would then be possible to achieve reliable and self-interested relations with the United States. The United States will recognize and respect the interests of Canada when Canada defines and develops her own destiny.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised indeed upon reading the motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) to find it was so unclear. It was difficult to see what he was driving at. This is not like the hon. gentleman who is usually so clear and concise that there is no misunderstanding. What he means is usually what he says.
As I understand the motion, it condemns the government for failing to foster closer economic and political relations with the United States and at the same time it blames the government for failing to develop economic and political independence of the United States. This is the old story-be damned if you do, and be damned if you don't. I wonder which of the condemnations the hon. member really means.
Economic Relations with United States
Let us deal with the first. Canada has traditionally had close economic relations with the United States. In fact, about 70 per cent of Canada's trade is with the United States. So how much closer do hon. members want Canada to get to the United States? In effect, the United States has provided Canada with needed investment capital and expertise. It has also provided Canada with a ready market for goods and products of all kinds. As a result, Canada has had and still enjoys a standard of living considered the second highest in the world, second only to that of the United States.
It is true, as was stated in a recent study by the Ontario Federation of Labour, that 138 plants were shut down in Ontario between June, 1970, and June, 1971. It was also true that 55 per cent were foreign-owned and controlled and employed about 63 per cent of the workers who were laid off or had their jobs made redundant. However, it is to be remembered that the other 45 per cent of the plants shut down, which accounted for the 37 per cent of the employees who lost their jobs, were under Canadian ownership and control.
Can you say with any degree of certainty, Mr. Speaker, that it is United States influence that has closed these plants when there were wholly-owned Canadian plants that shut down also? Do not the percentages I have quoted merely represent the degree of United States influence in Canada's economy? Surely you would not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when a business is not viable it should continue until bankruptcy results.
When President Nixon of the United States announced his new economic rules, the Canadian government immediately sent off a ministerial mission to see whether Canada could get an exemption. But to no avail. The United States was advised of Canada's position. It was pointed out that the 10 per cent surcharge on imports would fall particularly heavily on us because of our large volume of trade with the United States. Other countries made representations because they also are affected by the surcharge, such as Japan, France, West Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and others. Canada was not singled out for specially tough treatment; nor was Canada singled out for special consideration, in spite of our traditional trade arrangements with the United States. Nearly every country is affected by the 10 per cent surcharge, and no special exemptions have been granted, that I know of, apart from the quota on Japanese textiles.
What about the second condemnation contained in the motion, namely, the government's failure to foster economic and political independence from the United States? Surely the hon. member is aware of the government's desire to find other markets besides the United States on whom Canada has economic dependence. Canada stands to lose its preferred position with the United Kingdom with the impending entry of the U.K. into the European Common Market. Canada now stands to lose its preferred position in the United States market due to the 10 per cent surcharge. Obviously there is a moving away by Canada from dependence to economic independence.
Since this government took office there has been a concerted effort to find new friends and new markets throughout the world. Hence the diplomatic ties with

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
China, the Soviet Union and many other countries where alternative markets for Canada's goods and produce can be found. If that is not tantamount to fostering economic independence, then I do not know what is.
The fact is that in political and international affairs Canada has been ahead of the United States. It is only now that the United States is following Canada's lead. For example, the U.S. is planning to send its President to China and the Soviet Union. The fact, also, is that in times of economic crises, of tremendous inflation and unemployment, this government has been far ahead of the United States in reducing the inflation spiral and in taking steps to alleviate unemployment through additional benefits by way of unemployment insurance, manpower retraining schemes and other manpower programs.
It is a fact that further government action was taken with regard to prices and incomes through the establishment of the Prices and Incomes Commission. This kind of action is only now being taken in the United States. It is also the fact that at a time when the United States is taking protectionist measures and has applied a 10 per cent surcharge on imports to achieve economic survival, Canada did not sit idly by and do nothing. Canada did not break into tears or wring its hands. No-it did none of these things; rather, it took decisive action. It provided $80 million in federal aid to surcharge-smitten industries. It provided $1 billion infusion into the economy by way of a host of programs to help the country immeasurably and to assist in warding off the effects of the United States surcharge.
This government realizes that the surcharge could be retained for a considerable period of time, that it could even be increased and that further action may be taken by the United States to bolster its ailing dollar position. This government will take positive, decisive, action as deemed necessary to protect our economy and to maintain our high standard of living.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy that the House leader of the Conservative party has stood in his place and admitted this great error that his party has committed. He admits it is a very slanderous thing. It is also a very curious motion and I think points up some of the divisions within the Conservative party. They realize that there is a great feeling in this country of nationalism, a desire to develop an independent foreign and economic policy. Certain members of that party are also paranoiac when it comes to being anti-Communist or anti-anything that might offend the United States. In fact, one of the people very close to the nerve centre of the Conservative party told one of my colleagues that they had to include the first part in the motion to appease certain extremist elements within their party. I think perhaps this goes a long way to explain why this type of motion is before the House today.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the hon. member for Hillsborough should move a motion like this because I did not think he was that sort of person. I thought he was a man who saw the world in a more global way. I thought he was a man who took a more progressive attitude to international and domestic affairs. This type of motion totally breaks with the traditions of the Conservative party, from the time of Sir John A. Macdonald to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has been very conspicuous by his absence.
We all remember very well the general election campaigns of 1962 and 1963 when that right hon. gentleman was accused of being anti-American. Some of my constituents who voted for the Conservative party at that time would be very curious now about this motion. One reason they voted for the Conservative party was that the leader of the party at that time was a Canadian. He was talking about Canada asserting itself and he took the odd swipe at some of the multinational corporations. Then all of a sudden something happened to that party. A fellow named Dalton Camp came along, and so did a few Bay Street Tories, and the motion now before the House proves to me and to my constituents, no doubt, the many suspicions they had about the new Tory party-a party that has changed, that is now different, a party that is continentalist, a party that now wants to cosy up even more to the United States than it has in the past.
I think this motion was moved for a number of reasons. I do not doubt the sincerity of some members of the Conservative party and I do not criticize members such as the hon. members for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and Egmont (Mr. MacDonald). One of the bases on which the motion was moved is political opportunism. The Conservatives have sensed there is a bit of emotion in the country because of the visit of the Soviet Premier, perhaps because of the visit of the President of Yugoslavia, and other things. They are trying to play upon the emotions of a number of people who have genuine fear because of things that happened in the past.
Some people have suggested there may be an aura of McCarthyism developing in this country. This is not being helped by the motion before us today. Perhaps there is another reason for moving this motion. Perhaps the Con-
November 4, 1971

servatives are looking toward the next federal election. They will need a lot of money to finance a big campaign. Perhaps they are considering what happened in Ontario, where the money comes from for their elections. I think a motion like this may have been drafted with that in mind. Perhaps they hired a public relations man from Michigan to help them draft this motion with a view to convincing the Canadian people. This is the type of motion we often see from the Conservative party.

The hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) is making his typical remarks in a debate of this kind.
A number of things have brought about this motion. The Conservative party has been very concerned about our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) visiting the Soviet Union and signing a protocol with them. People were concerned about the visit of Premier Kosygin to Canada because this might alienate us from the United States. Mr. Kosygin went to the United States, yet still people in this country are concerned about his visit here. They are also concerned about the visit of Mr. Tito. He was also in the United States a few days ago.
In this House we have some intellectual dinosaurs in the Conservative party crying about the Taiwan situation and nationalist China being seated in the United Nations. We failed to recognize the People's Republic of China for 20 years, but at least we have recognized that they are in existence. The French recognized them in 1949.

speechtext:
If I am in the House as long as the hon. member for Oxford and begin to support the suggestions and policies he supports, I shall be glad to leave. We must continue in the direction of improving our foreign affairs. We must try to make the United Nations a universal body, giving it more power and sovereignty. We must continue in that direction. I commend the government of Canada and members of my party as well as others who have tried to convince governments for years to move in that direction.
There are a number of other things that might be said in this debate. The second part of the motion does raise some concern regarding the economic policy of Canada. It is about time we in Canada developed an economy which is independent in order that we can make our own decisions, provide more jobs and not be a branch plant of another country, or a multinational corporation. This is the direction in which we must move and we must do so soon if Canada is to continue as a nation.
The only industries we actually control in Canada are the broadcasting industry, the banking industry and the booze industry. That is a sad commentary on the wellbeing of this country. The sad thing is that the Americans do not come in with only their money. The United States department of commerce has issued a statement to the effect that over 90 per cent of foreign investment by multinational companies in Canada have used Canadian money generated in Canada by plants operated here or generated on the Canadian financial market, so they are buying us out with our own money. We are losing jobs and a lot of our political sovereignty, and we are exporting more wealth than we are importing from the United States.
It is about time we in this country woke up and devised policies whereby Canadians can control their won destinies. That should be the main thrust of this debate. That is what the Conservative member for Fundy-Royal is concerned about and that is the concern of most Canadians from coast to coast. They are more concerned with this than with the phony issues dragged out by some of the more reactionary Tories in this House.

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP POLICIES TO ENSURE ECONOMIC INDEPENDENCE AND FULL EMPLOYMENT-DETERIORATION OF RELATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to say a few words about the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland). My party cannot support it, because we believe to do so would be to condone the government for what it has done and we feel what has been done has not been adequate.
In any debate such as this we must take a serious look at the point of view held by the United States and decide whether or not we agree or disagree with its position. We must remember, I believe, that before World War II the Americans were isolationist and were soundly denounced by many people in the western world, including Canadians. Since the end of World War II they have taken a most active part in the world and at the present time they feel they have ended up with fewer friends and find themselves disliked intensely in many parts of the world.
In their opinion they have aided the world a good deal since World War II. I think we can say that Germany and Japan, which were bankrupt, benefited a great deal from the Marshall aid plan which went a long way toward making those countries very aggressive in a commercial sense. The United States has carried the burden of an enormous defence in a nuclear world with little or no help from Germany, Japan, Canada and the western European countries. The United States has followed a policy of containment of Communism in the Viet Nam war. In the minds of historians, the Viet Nam war may well be viewed as the war that contained the Chinese communists until the red regime of Mao Tse-tung quieted down and lost some of its aggressiveness. Almost certainly, without the Viet Nam war Chinese Communism would be extending far into the South Pacific and most likely would have overwhelmed the Philippines and be lapping at the shores of Australia.
What has all this effort brought to the American nation from their own viewpoint? It has brought the United States into the situation of seriously reassessing its position. It is faced with a trade deficit of $13 billion. It is reassessing its position of defending for free the western world. It is increasingly aware of so-called interference by United States companies in the commercial world and the accusation that they are trying to buy up the world. As to the trading position of the United States, perhaps this can best be illustrated in the words of Maurice H. Stans, United States Secretary of Commerce who on October 27, 1971, said:
Our share of the world's international trade dropped from approximately 21 per cent to about 18 per cent within a decade.
In 1970 Germany replaced the United States as the world's leading exporter of manufactured goods.
Our trade in minerals and fuels and low technology goods are steadily moving deeper into very severe deficits.
Even our traditional dominance in high technology trade has begun to be challenged by a number of countries in a number of items, including electronics, computers and aircraft.
Other countries have begun investing relatively more than we are doing in plant assets, in research and development, and in incentives for technological achievements, and they enjoy substantially lower wage levels.
Over the past five years productivity in American industry has had the smallest increase of any industrial nation in the free world-far slower than our major competitors.

Finally, competing countries have confronted us with a large and growing array of trade barriers, investment restrictions and various violations of accepted international rules and agreements-all of which severely jeopardized our competitive position in the world, and undermined the strength of the dollar.
He continued:
Out of all these individual problems, several conclusions have become very clear! For one, the United States cannot go on absorbing the goods of the world, unless we are able to compete equally and fairly in the markets of the world. Secondly, the time has come for new international agreements on tariffs and trade, on the protection of foreign investment, on the elimination of non-tariff barriers, on uniform technical standards, and so on.
Whether we agree with this or not, these are the words of a responsible member of the United States government. But what has happened? During the last decade the foreign policy of Canada has shown a tendency to diverge from the United States. Since the advent of this administration the government of Canda has moved a remarkably long way in its difference of opinion with its American neighbour. The present administration has acted very much as if Canada were in orbit, spinning around sometimes very close to the Soviet Union.
In April, 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) downgraded Canada's role in the western collective security system and put stress on "protection of our sovereignty." By making a distinction between collective security arrangements and protection of our sovereignty, the Prime Minister revealed his ignorance of Canada's defence problems. Due to Canada's position, and especially since the advent of the nuclear era, we have to rely on the collective protection of other people. Since 1940 the mainstay of our security has been the North Atlantic Treaty Organization whose backbone has been the might of the United States. Had the United States wanted to do so, it could have swallowed us decades ago, the same as Russia has done with the Baltic states. The only real protection we have to our sovereignty is collective defence, and for self-evident reasons our well-being depends entirely on western collective security.
The white paper on defence states:
It is highly unlikely Canada would be attacked by a foreign power other than as a result of a strategic nuclear strike directed at the U.S.. .. Canada's overriding defence objective must therefore be the prevention of nuclear war . . . Because of Canada's obvious inability to deter major nuclear war unilaterally, we can best contribute to peace by participating in collective security arrangements.
The reduction of Canada's participation in NATO is well known and has made us suspect in all of western Europe. But as if this were not enough, in Singapore the Prime Minister next turned his attention to the British Commonwealth of Nations. There the Prime Minister effectively sided with the forces of India, Tanzania, Zambia and Uganda, all of whom are intimately connected with communist China against Great Britain.
Then in respect of the enormous Soviet menace in the Indian Ocean it was said that the Canadian delegates could care less if somebody pulled the plug from the Indian Ocean. Canada sided with those countries that were against the sale of British arms to South Africa, arms which could be used in the naval defence of the Indian Ocean, while at the same time it made little com-
November 4, 1971

ment on the sale of arms by France and Italy which could be directly used against villages and their inhabitants.
Then in May of this year the Prime Minister made a visit to the Soviet Union. The western world had too late prevented the communist enslavement of eastern and central Europe but had stopped Soviet expansion in the heart of the continent and stabilized a line of armed coexistence. It was not the western world but the communists who turned the dividing line into an ideological as well as a physical iron curtain with electrified barbed wire and machine-gun towers. It has turned the whole Soviet Union into a huge concentration camp. In his report to the Twenty-fourth Congress of the Soviet communist party on March 30 this year, Leonid Brezhnev said:
The full triumph of the socialist cause all over the world is inevitable. And we shall not spare ourselves in the fight for this triumph-
And what did the Prime Minister say about this? In a communique he issued the following astounding statement:
The discussions revealed that Canada and the U.S.S.R. hold similar views on a number of international problems.
Then there was his assertion in Kiev that Soviet and Canadian citizens were living under similar federal systems of government. Then there was his repeated allegation of acute United States "danger to our identity from the cultural, economic and perhaps even military point of view". The visit of Premier Kosygin, which might have been turned into a reasonable exchange between countries of different ideologies, was made the occasion to launch an attack by Mr. Kosygin on the economic policies of the United States.
Now we have the surcharge of August 15. For many years economic nationalists in Canada have been busily claiming that the Americans are making us hewers of wood and drawers of water. This has been the cry in many quarters of central Canada. It has been the cry of the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans)-and I do not put any more stock in what he said about this than I do in his running of the Post Office. The Prime Minister recently said that if the Americans do realize what they are doing, and if it becomes apparent that they want us to be just "sellers of natural resources to them and buyers of their manufactured goods, we will have to reassess fundamentally our relations with them, trading, political and otherwise".
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), on September 7 while speaking in the House of Commons on President Nixon's surcharge, said that 85 per cent of exports of Canadian finished goods are sold in the United States. Surely this rejects the Prime Minister's view that Canadians are treated as hewers of wood and drawers of water. Our export statistics show that in 1969 Canada sold abroad highly-finished industrial products worth $5,630 million. Of this total, 86.8 per cent went to the United States, 1.78 per cent to the European Common Market and 1.4 per cent to the United Kingdom. Excluding the United States market, we have sold only 13.2 per cent of our export manufactured goods to other countries. In 1969 the export total of $14.87 billion bears the classification of processed industrial materials. Here the labour content is lower but it is still substantial. We sold $5,251 million worth of processed industrial materials abroad. Of this
Economic Relations with United States
total, 69.5 per cent went to the United States, 10.2 per cent to the United Kingdom and 6 per cent to the European Common Market. Canada's exports now total $17.5 billion, of whiph 75 per cent goes to the United States.
Those who say, including the Prime Minister, that the Americans just want us to be "sellers of natural resources to them and buyers of their manufactured products" must realize, surely, that this does not bear up under examination. The United Kingdom, the European Common Market and Japan have been getting raw materials from Canada without providing any substantial outlet for any industrial goods. Indeed, Japan is noted for this. If Washington had always had its own interest at heart, why would it have signed the auto pact agreement when the United States had $704 million surplus in 1965 which has been turned into $1,200 million in favour of Canada this year?
If it is true that the government hopes to replace the United States in exports to the Soviet Union, let us take a look at trade last year. We sold $128 million to the Soviet Union, mostly in wheat, and took back $8 million. The energy talks which have been suspended by the United States after the outburst of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) have not been resumed. Communications between Washington and Ottawa are at a low ebb. Apparently the Prime Minister has forgotten that Washington has an enormous political and economic clout and that their influence could have a severe impact on the Canadian economy.
No one knows what the new measures of phase 2 in the Nixon administration will be, but it is likely that they will be no less severe than the surcharge. This may well require some hard bargaining over the auto pact. There may have to be bargaining over the sale of energy, and if so what will the amounts be? We have energy for sale but it is high-priced energy and the only buyers can be the Americans. We will have to decide whether or not we will sell them any more.
With regard to the larger issues, Canadians will have to do some deciding with regard to their future course of action. Almost certainly the United States is entering a period of trade protectionism and is withdrawing within its own borders. The United States has the resources to provide its people with a reasonable standard of living. We must decide if Canada wishes to accept the premise of Economic nationalism with restrictions on foreign capital and with the consequent restriction in job expansion in the immediate future.
The reports would indicate that the unpublished Gray report pursues a policy of restrictions on foreign capital. We will have the fastest growing labour force in the western world in the next decade. We have built up the most comprehensive welfare system, in its broadest sense, in the western world which is still increasing its share of the take of the gross national product. The Unemployment Insurance Act goes a long way toward guaranteed income and provides 44 weeks of benefit for eight weeks of work. The tax bill presently before the House will restrict the development of the resource industries and channel investment money to manufacturing. That area will

November 4, 1971
Economic Relations with United States
increasingly feel shut out from its only real market by the action of the United States.
It is widely stated that the new competition act and the labour act will restrict business growth. These will have to be considered extremely carefully. Canada will have to assess whether it wishes to have closer trading arrangements with the United States or revert to a more independent status. If the United Kingdom, with its population of 55 million, feels it has to join the Common Market, surely the importance of trade with the U.S. and whatever results it might have will require considerable debate by Canadians.
Under the present administration there will be no meaningful dialogue between Canada and the United States regarding these problems. Dialogue with the United States will be at a relative standstill until this government is replaced.

I do not know how many hon. members live as close to the border as I do, that is, two or three miles. I live in a great area where tourism is important. I live in an area where we mingle with our friends from the south. They come to our area and we travel back and forth. We have learned to understand each other.
I would like to say at the outset that I do not know of any man who has received as many compliments for being an out-and-out courageous individual, one who is really intent on being a statesman in our country. These are the statements that have been made to me by our American friends, statements directed at our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).

You do not create it with words or with rhetoric. You create it with hard work to contribute to the gross national product with something that you can sell.
(Mr. Ritchie.]
We have not yet found a way to provide the standard of living which we have in Canada without selling something, without trading with people, without initiating a manufactured product or at least a type of product. True, our natural resources are basic. We know that mining, lumbering and farming are our basic industries. Out of this grows our gross national product, the service industries and everything else. This is all very well, but first we must have markets and, as we know, our problem in agriculture has never been production. We have in Canada the most efficient agricultural industry in the world, but our problem is markets. We must realize that without the United States we are confined so far as our markets are concerned.
I agree that a minority element in Canada is attempting to drive a wedge between us but I submit that they are not impressing our American friends, although they are treading a dangerous path, apparently supported by the NDP. What they say is utter nonsense. Now they attempt to condemn us for acting responsibly. They keep jumping from one side of the fence to the other, hoping the political climate will somehow improve and assist the lost cause of their party which has been searching in vain for ten years to find anything on which to hang a hope.
Of course, the Americans are tough traders. Those of us who have been involved in doing business with our American friends know full well that when one deals with an American one had better be careful, because they are pastmasters in the art of making a buck. That is what has made them great. This is not confined to Canada. Those who would suggest to the Canadian people that the Americans are simply interested in making investments in Canada for the purpose of taking it over should consider the fact that 52 per cent of the assets of the world are at least partly owned by the United States of America.
I can recall reading in history books of the time when England, that small island, sent out her merchant ships all over the world to take the products of the rest of the world back to England, from where they were traded to the nations of the world. They did a fine, a fantastic job. They opened the trade routes of the world. They created the necessary basis for trade, which is so essential to all of us. I wonder how many of us really know how much British investment there still is in Canada. Just a year or two ago the Hudson Bay Company decided it was time to transfer its head office to Canada, where the company's principal operation has always been and where its money has been made. I can recall that when I worked in the Bank of Montreal, every Thursday I had to send a state-
November 4, 1971

ment to Threadneedle Street in London. I know that the CPR did not do that well just on Canadian investment; it needed the help of British investment.
Suddenly it is now suggested by the opposition, I believe for purely political expediency, that we are taking a whack at the United States of America. In reply I say that suddenly we have been confronted with a problem. Every day businessmen are confronted with these problems. Suddenly a good customer decides that he is too good a customer, or he is actually in trouble. He decides that maybe he has overextended. Anybody in business who has been in a position of overextension knows how difficult this can be.
I suggest that the Americans today could be rather overextended in their investments throughout the world and that their money is having a little problem because of that fact. They have been going out into the nations of the world investing their money, not entirely because they want to assist the rest of the world but because by investing in other areas they may find labour that is cheaper and raw materials which are easier to obtain. Any sound businessman investing in anything is not doing it for others, but for himself.
